Myths that sound scientific

Do blind people hear better?

Their ears are not sharper, but their brains can make better use of what they hear, especially if blindness began early.

It is widely believed that losing sight sharpens the other senses. It is partly true, but not in the ear itself: the hearing threshold, the faintest sound that can be detected, is similar.

A brain that reorganises

What changes is how information is processed. In people blind from birth or early childhood, the visual cortex becomes active when they listen or read braille. A 2004 study found that early-blind people distinguished changes in pitch better than sighted people, and many more had absolute pitch.

Some blind people even learn echolocation: they click their tongue and, from the echo, perceive the distance and shape of objects. These skills are not automatic; they develop with practice and come more easily the earlier blindness begins.

References

  1. Gougoux, F. et al. (2004). Pitch discrimination in the early blind. Nature, 430(6997), 309.
  2. Thaler, L., Arnott, S. R. y Goodale, M. A. (2011). Neural correlates of natural human echolocation in early and late blind echolocation experts. PLoS ONE, 6(5), e20162.
